questions.question: The order of a difference equation for a sequence $(x_t)_{t\ge0}$ is the gap between the largest and the smallest time index that occur. What is the order of $x_{t+4}=3x_{t+2}-x_{t+1}$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$?
options: Undefined, because $x_t$ itself does not occur

questions.question: A difference equation is linear if it can be written as $x_{t+k}+a_{k-1}(t)x_{t+k-1}+\cdots+a_0(t)x_t=g_t$ with $a_0(t)\ne0$. Which of the following equations, for $t=0,1,2,\dots$, is linear?

Consider the linear difference equation $x_{t+1}=2x_t+3$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$, and the set of all its real solutions $(x_t)_{t\ge0}$ with termwise addition and scalar multiplication. Is this set a vector space?
options: No: the constant term $3$ makes the equation nonlinear.
Yes: the sum of two solutions is again a solution.
Yes: every initial value $x_0$ gives exactly one solution.
No: the zero sequence is not a solution, since $0\ne2\cdot0+3$.

questions.question: For a difference equation $x_{t+k}=f(t,x_t,\ldots,x_{t+k-1})$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$, which sequence is called an equilibrium (steady state)?
options: The value $x^*$ that every solution approaches as $t\to\infty$
Any solution that stays bounded for all times $t\ge0$
A constant sequence $x_t=x^*$ that solves the equation
A value $x^*$ at which the right-hand side $f$ equals zero

questions.question: A difference equation of order $3$ is given in the explicit form $x_{t+3}=f(t,x_t,x_{t+1},x_{t+2})$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$, with $f$ defined everywhere. Which prescribed data determine exactly one solution?
The sequence $(x_t)$ satisfies $x_{t+2}=x_{t+1}+2x_t$ for $t=0,1,2,\dots$ with $x_0=1$ and $x_1=0$. Computing recursively, what is $x_4$?
With the forward difference $\Delta x_t=x_{t+1}-x_t$, a balance obeys $\Delta x_t=-0.2\,x_t+5$ for $t=0,1,2,\dots$. Which shifted form is the same difference equation?
What is the equilibrium $x^*$ of the difference equation $x_{t+1}=0.5\,x_t+4$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$?
For the nonlinear difference equation $x_{t+1}=3x_t(1-x_t)$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$, which values are all of its equilibria?
A solution of $x_{t+1}=2x_t-1$ must satisfy the relation for every $t=0,1,2,\dots$. Which sequence $(x_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a solution?
In the linear form $x_{t+k}+a_{k-1}(t)x_{t+k-1}+\cdots+a_0(t)x_t=g_t$ of a difference equation of order $k$, the coefficient must satisfy $a_0(t)\ne0$ for all $t$. Why is this condition imposed?
options: It makes the equation homogeneous, so that its solutions form a vector space.
It is needed for $x_0,\ldots,x_{k-1}$ to determine exactly one solution.
It guarantees that the equation has an equilibrium $x^*$.
If $a_0(t)=0$, then $x_t$ would not occur and the order would be below $k$.

questions.question: Let $p$ be one solution of a linear difference equation $x_{t+k}+a_{k-1}(t)x_{t+k-1}+\cdots+a_0(t)x_t=g_t$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$. Which description gives all of its solutions?
options: $p+h$, where $h$ runs through the solutions of the equation with $g_t=0$
$p+c$, where $c$ runs through all constant sequences
$c\,p$, where $c$ runs through all real numbers
$p+h$, where $h$ runs through the solutions of the same equation

questions.question: How is the difference equation $x_{t+2}-3x_{t+1}+2x_t=t$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$, correctly classified?
options: Linear, inhomogeneous, of order $2$, with non-constant coefficients
Nonlinear, since the variable $t$ appears explicitly
Linear and homogeneous, since no constant term is present
Linear, inhomogeneous, of order $2$, with constant coefficients

questions.question: A second-order linear difference equation reads $x_{t+2}-x_{t+1}+0.5\,x_t=3$ for $t=0,1,2,\dots$. Which constant sequence $x_t=x^*$ solves it?
Which statement about the equilibria of the difference equation $x_{t+1}=x_t+2$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$, is correct?
options: $x^*=0$, as for every linear difference equation.
Every constant is one, since $x_{t+1}-x_t$ is constant.
There is none, since $x^*=x^*+2$ has no solution.

questions.question: Consider $x_{t+1}=x_t^2$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$, with initial value $x_0=-1$. Which statement about this solution and the equilibria of the equation is correct?
options: It is an equilibrium solution, since its values are constant from $t=1$ onwards.
It is the constant sequence $-1$, since $-1$ is an equilibrium of the equation.
It is $-1,1,1,1,\dots$: it reaches the equilibrium $1$ but is not an equilibrium solution.
It is not uniquely determined, since $x_1^2$ and $x_1$ can have two values.

questions.question: For an explicit equation $x_{t+k}=f(t,x_t,\ldots,x_{t+k-1})$, $k$ initial values determine exactly one solution. Why can this fail for the relation $x_{t+1}^2=x_t^2$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$, with $x_0=1$?
options: Both $1,1,1,\dots$ and $1,-1,1,-1,\dots$ satisfy it, since $x_{t+1}$ is not given explicitly.
It has order $2$, because of the squares, so one initial value is too few.
It is nonlinear, and nonlinear equations have no solution for a given $x_0$.
It has no solution with $x_0=1$, since $x_1^2=1$ has no real root.

questions.question: The equation $x_{t+1}=x_t^2$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$, has no term $g_t$ on its right-hand side. Is its set of real solutions a vector space under termwise addition and scalar multiplication?
options: No: the zero sequence is not a solution of the equation.
No: the constant $1$ is a solution, but $1+1=2$ is not.
Yes: it has no term $g_t$, so it is homogeneous.
Yes: each value $x_0$ determines exactly one solution.

questions.question: Let $\Delta x_t=x_{t+1}-x_t$ and $\Delta^2x_t=\Delta x_{t+1}-\Delta x_t$. Written with shifted terms, what is the equation $\Delta^2x_t+\Delta x_t=0$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$, and its order?
Two sequences $u$ and $v$ both solve $x_{t+2}-x_{t+1}-x_t=1$, $t=0,1,2,\dots$. Which of the following sequences is guaranteed to solve the same equation?
